title: Show me one
hookLine: show me someone ill and happy, in danger and happy: show me a Stoic (Discourses 2.19)

cards: Somebody at a party explains, in great detail, the whole theory of mindfulness. Five minutes later they're furious at the bartender. The theory was flawless.
The bartender saw none of it. Knowing the words is one thing; living them is another. Epictetus had students who could talk their way through Stoic arguments with ease.
In one talk he turns on them, and asks for something no amount of reciting could fake.

teach.b: This is Discourses book two, chapter nineteen. It opens with a well-known puzzle in logic, the Master Argument, and the people who show off by discussing it. Epictetus lets them talk, and then turns.
You can all recite the arguments, he says. So who among you is a Stoic?

teach.h: SHAPED LIKE A STATUE BY PHIDIAS.
teach.b: We call a statue Phidian when it's shaped by Phidias' art. Show me a person shaped by the beliefs they talk about. Then the list.

teach.h: SICK AND HAPPY, EXILED AND HAPPY.
teach.b: Show me someone who is sick, and happy. In danger, and happy. Dying, and happy.
Exiled, and happy. Disgraced, and happy. Show me!
By the gods, he says, I long to see a Stoic. Then he does something disarming. He lowers the bar.
You can't show me one who's finished, he admits.
Then show me one who's being shaped, who has started leaning that way. Do an old man a favor. Don't keep from me a sight I've never yet seen.
Sit with that. A Stoic teacher says he has never yet seen a finished Stoic.
That's not despair. It's the honesty that keeps the whole thing real. Nobody here is finished.
The question is only whether you're being shaped, whether someone watching you on a hard day could see the arguments turning into a person. Not the whole statue. One recognizable line of it.

how: Some readers of Epictetus judge their practice less by what they know about Stoicism than by how they act on an ordinary hard day.

o: a teacher's rule that his students must obey
a well-known logic puzzle, recited by students showing off
the final debate a student must win to graduate

p: sick and happy, exiled and happy
had never seen a finished one

s: Epictetus says he has met many finished Stoics
he says he longs to see one, and has never yet seen the sight.
he lowers the bar to someone who is being shaped
show me one who has started leaning that way.
Epictetus was impressed by his students' logic
he turns from their arguments to ask who actually lives them.

games.q: a student proudly recites a well-known logic puzzle. you're Epictetus. what do you ask?
o: show me someone shaped by these beliefs: sick and happy, exiled and happy.
games.why: he asks to see a Stoic in the flesh, then softens it: show me one who's being shaped, a sight he says he's never seen.

practice: Pick one thing you believe about how to live: be patient, be honest, don't panic over what you can't control. Picture a small hard moment ahead, a delay, a criticism, bad news, and someone watching you in it.
Not perfection; just one visible line of what you believe, and you showing it.

wordCard.voice: Master Argument. The puzzle in logic that opens this talk, after which Epictetus turns on his students who can recite every argument and asks: who among you is a Stoic?

carryVoice: Your line: one who's being shaped. Not finished, just leaning the right way. Day four hundred fourteen.
